newsitem.title: USA: Near-record U.S. crops deflate food price fears.
newsitem.headline: Near-record U.S. crops deflate food price fears.

text.p: Ideal fall weather sharply boosted the size of near-record U.S. corn and soybean crops, easing fears of a surge in food prices, the Agriculture Department said on Tuesday.

It forecast a corn crop of 9.27 billion bushels, the third-largest on record and 3 percent larger than its October estimate. The soybean harvest was pegged at 2.40 billion bushels, the second-largest crop ever, up 2 percent.
Stockpiles would remain tight, however, making another large crop vital in 1997, the department said.

Large U.S. crops should hold food price inflation to 4 percent or so this year and perhaps as low as 3 percent in 1997, analysts said, far lower than was projected in mid-summer, when the outlook was worrisome and grain prices soared. Crops were slowed by a wet spring and cool summer, but were blessed by warm, sunny weather in the final weeks prior to the harvest.
"It just got to the edge of being serious, and then the crops got good," said private consultant John Schnittker. "It was an amazing fall."

Corn and soybean prices fell quickly when trading in futures contracts opened at the Chicago Board of Trade two hours after the USDA report was issued. The updated crop forecasts were larger than traders expected, and corn for December delivery was down 5 cents a bushel to $2.63-3/4 and November soybeans fell 14 cents to $6.66 a bushel.
"Everything is bearish. The bean number was up and the corn number was up," said Ron Kucha of O'Connor and Co.
"It looks like a pretty dismal picture for corn (prices)," said Gregg Hunt of the Chicago trading house Rand Financial Services. "I believe new lows will be made."
Schnittker said corn prices might fall below $2.50 a bushel in Chicago as the grain markets adjusted.

Based on Nov. 1 conditions, the Agriculture Department raised its forecast of corn yields in all major states and said the crop would average 126.5 bushels an acre nationwide, up 3.5 bushels in a month. Soybean yields were up 0.9 bushel an acre for a projected 37.9 bushels per acre, due to "nearly ideal weather."
Heavy demand at home and abroad was forecast to consume most of the huge output, leaving little cushion against a shortfall next year.
About 210 million bushels of soybeans will be on hand when the 1997 harvest begins, the department said, and 1.1 billion bushels of corn.
The corn "carryover" would be more than twice as large as this fall, but still 30 percent lower than 1995's level.

Cotton output was estimated at 18.59 million bales, the third-highest ever and up 400,000 bales from October due to improved yields, now forecast for 698 pounds per acre. There are 480 pounds in a bale.

The updated figures underscored how the decade has become one of bin-busting crops for U.S. farmers. The three largest corn crops have been grown this decade, the two largest soybean crops and two of the three largest cotton crops. The No. 3 wheat crop was grown in 1990.
